segments.title: The treaty uncertainty behind a forgotten battleship generation
segments.body: The opening places these studies between the better-known G3, F3, and N3 projects and the later King George V, Lion, and Vanguard generation. Uncertainty over whether the Washington treaty system would survive after 1930 gave the Royal Navy a reason to keep alternative capital-ship plans ready. The surviving archive is asymmetrical: detailed smaller schemes are plentiful, while information about 35,000-ton designs with sixteen-inch guns is sparse. Remarks by Stanley Goodall, Henderson, other Third Sea Lords, and Directors of Naval Construction suggest that larger concepts once existed. Repeatedly scaling similar layouts across different gun sizes, together with strategic papers demanding rapid worldwide response, makes the uniformly slow surviving designs look incomplete. The uneven record shows how historians combine surviving plans, institutional practice, and contemporary strategy without presenting inference as fact.

evidence.note: The transcript defines the forgotten interwar generation and links its design work to uncertainty over what would follow the Washington treaty system.
Abundant records survive for smaller schemes, while sparse evidence for 35,000-ton sixteen-inch designs requires historical inference.
Hints of larger designs accompany a mismatch between the slow documented ships and the strategic demand for rapid global response.

segments.summary: Uncertainty over the naval treaty system prompted the Royal Navy to study a largely forgotten generation of capital ships before 1930, including designs whose surviving record may be incomplete.

segments.title: Political economy collides with credible capital-ship design
segments.body: The Admiralty was the whole government department, including political leaders, professional Sea Lords, and constructors. Election-cycle incentives encouraged immediate savings even when replacing ships, building infrastructure, and training people could take two or three political cycles. An options paper might give ministers several choices, yet Treasury pressure could still make the cheapest one politically attractive. Credit flowing upward while blame moved downward meant naval officers had to plan for the consequences of that choice. A Third Sea Lord or constructor might later command the fleet that received these ships, while an older HMS Warspite could outfight the weakest proposals. Designs with protection inferior to existing capital ships therefore look less like professional preferences than evidence of political pressure pushing the design staff toward a dangerous minimum.

evidence.note: The transcript separates political pressure for economy from the preferences of professional naval officers.
Election-cycle savings conflicted with long procurement lead times, while ministers could choose the cheapest option and pass responsibility down the chain.
The transcript tests the cheaper concepts against existing capital ships and the responsibility borne by constructors and Sea Lords.

segments.summary: Pressure for cheaper battleships came especially from political leaders, while naval constructors and admirals still had to produce ships capable of surviving against existing heavily armed opponents.

segments.title: Continuous design work preserves a navy's ability to respond
segments.body: The 1925 and 1926 capital-ship studies largely explored changes to Nelson and Rodney, and the work continued even without a funded building program. Separate cruiser, carrier, capital-ship, and destroyer studies ran alongside plans for modernizing ships already in service. The value becomes clear in the urgent flagship example: a current study could be polished in days so a yard began work within a week, rather than spending months restarting design from scratch. That responsiveness mattered when an admiral had only about five months to make a ship ready. Continuous work also kept enough skilled constructors together and gave their teams practice during pauses in construction. Design readiness was a standing institutional capability rather than a document prepared only after procurement began.

evidence.note: Continuous design-study programs across several warship types and existing-ship modernization.
Current design studies preserved constructor skills and enabled yards to respond quickly when orders arrived.

segments.summary: Royal Navy constructors kept cruiser, carrier, capital-ship, destroyer, and modernization studies active even without an immediate building program, preserving skills and shortening emergency response times.

segments.title: The 1927 designs search for a minimum viable battleship
segments.body: The January design used nine fourteen-inch guns in three triple turrets, while the June version used eight in four twins. Both retained 45,000 shaft horsepower and were credited with about twenty-three knots despite their different hull lengths, which makes the repeated speed figure questionable. Shorter, narrower, and shallower hulls saved roughly 5,800 tons against Nelson and Rodney in the closest comparison. The saving came with a twelve-inch main belt and fourteen-inch turret faces, leaving protection below both the Nelson class and the later King George V class. Because no arrangement drawings survive with the tables, the illustrated F3-style or Nelson-style layouts remain possibilities rather than established reconstructions. The studies are most useful as a minimum viable baseline whose economy would expose the ships to older heavy-gun opponents.

evidence.note: The January 1927 study paired nine 14-inch guns in three triple turrets with 45,000 shaft horsepower, while the shorter June design used eight guns in four twin turrets; both studies assigned about 23 knots to ships with lighter armor than Nelson and Rodney.
Compared with Nelson, Rodney, and the later King George V class, the compact designs appear to be a minimum baseline.

segments.summary: Two 1927 studies paired fourteen-inch guns with compact hulls and reduced protection, creating cheaper ships that look like a dangerous baseline rather than convincing successors to Nelson and Rodney.

segments.title: Missing sixteen-inch studies expose gaps in the design record
segments.body: The available drawings point toward forward sixteen-inch main armament, aircraft-handling facilities aft, and more than one possible distribution of the six-inch secondary battery. Even the anti-aircraft fit is uncertain because surviving illustrations show four-inch singles while the surrounding discussion refers to twin 4.7-inch weapons. No accompanying table preserves displacement, machinery power, speed, or protection, so rough scaling cannot support firm data. Admiralty comparison tables can survive in standard archival forms, but unbuilt designs never generated the more detailed and systematically organized yard drawings produced for construction. The result is a reconstruction problem in which missing tables and drawings limit what can safely be said. This moment shows where a naval historian must separate visible design features from inference.

evidence.note: Sixteen-inch drawings whose performance and protection statistics do not survive.
Because unbuilt designs never generated the systematic yard drawings prepared for construction, their surviving record can lack the tables and details available for ships that reached a builder.

segments.summary: Surviving drawings show sixteen-inch concepts without their statistical tables, illustrating how incomplete archives complicate efforts to reconstruct the Royal Navy's interwar capital-ship thinking.

segments.title: Design 16A favors twin-turret survivability at treaty displacement
segments.body: Design 16A closely matched Nelson and Rodney in beam and draft but used a longer hull on a 35,000-ton standard displacement. Its 45,000-shaft-horsepower plant delivered only twenty-three knots, while four twin turrets carried eight sixteen-inch guns alongside six twin six-inch mounts and four twin high-angle 4.7-inch mounts. Protection included a thirteen-inch belt abreast the magazines, an eleven-inch belt abreast machinery, heavy deck armor, and a one-and-a-half-inch torpedo bulkhead. The letter suffix matters because the Royal Navy's numbering system implies that at least one other sixteen-inch variant once existed. Four twins also improved damage tolerance: one disabled turret removed one quarter of the main battery rather than one third. That survivability choice cost substantial weight: compared with Nelson and Rodney, 16A was about 1,200 tons heavier and roughly thirty feet longer while carrying one fewer main gun.

evidence.note: 16A's dimensions, machinery, armament, protection, and 35,000-ton standard displacement.
The transcript infers additional variants from the design name and explains the survivability logic of four twin turrets.

segments.summary: The 35,000-ton 16A design combined eight sixteen-inch guns in four twin turrets with twenty-three-knot speed, sacrificing one gun to reduce the firepower lost when a turret was disabled.

segments.title: Fourteen-inch designs trade armor and weight for speed
segments.body: Compared with 16A, the fourteen-inch alternatives retained eight guns in four twin turrets but cut both displacement and armor. Their machinery rose from 45,000 to roughly 60,000-plus shaft horsepower, making the missing speed figure in the surviving table especially conspicuous. The longer 14A had a more favorable length-to-beam ratio than 14B, leading to an estimated speed of about twenty-seven or twenty-eight knots. A longer, narrower hull moves more efficiently at cruising speed but creates more area to armor, whereas a shorter proportion favors maneuverability. The quoted belt figures also describe layered protection, with extra internal plate over the magazines rather than one uniformly thick belt. This comparison turns an incomplete table into a compact lesson on how hull proportions, machinery, armor, and weight interact.

evidence.note: The fourteen-inch designs' dimensions and machinery permit only an inferred speed because the surviving table omits the exact figure.
The quoted belt figures describe layered protection over the magazines, while the fourteen-inch designs retained four twin turrets.

segments.summary: The 14A and 14B studies cut displacement and armor while sharply increasing machinery power, suggesting a faster battleship whose exact speed is absent from the surviving table.

segments.title: Small-gun treaty battleships face a fatal mismatch
segments.body: The Royal Navy explored a wide family of twelve-, eleven-, and ten-inch-gun designs in order to discover how far treaty limits could be pushed downward. Some carried only ten inches of belt armor, less than HMS Dreadnought, while most lacked enough speed to escape IJN Nagato and only a few could outrun the slower Colorado class. Design 11A, for example, placed eight eleven-inch guns in four twin turrets on about 23,300 tons. Such a ship becomes coherent only if every power accepts the same restrictions and older heavy units are removed. A modernized HMS Hood would dominate new eleven-inch opponents that could catch her, while Nagato would do the same to British equivalents. The exercise exposes a transition problem in arms control: a lighter future fleet is unsafe while even a handful of older or noncompliant heavy ships remains.

evidence.note: The transcript reviews the thin armor of the smaller-gun studies and compares them with existing heavy battleships.
The broad small-gun design family remained vulnerable because Hood and Nagato would upset an eleven-inch-gun treaty system.

segments.summary: Studies armed with twelve-, eleven-, or ten-inch guns could satisfy ambitions for tighter treaty limits, but their thin armor and inability to escape ships such as Nagato made them dangerous unless every existing heavy capital ship disappeared.

segments.title: Air-power treaties reveal the limits of arms control
segments.body: Failed efforts to limit air power illustrate the wider problem of treaty definitions. A civilian airliner could be designed for rapid conversion into a bomber, making a simple ban on bomber aircraft easy to evade. Eliminating bombers would also undermine the rationale for fighters, while retaining ground-attack aircraft would recreate much of the prohibited capability under another name. The example clarifies why naval treaties relied on measurable categories such as gun calibre and displacement yet still produced complicated rules and strategically awkward ship designs.

evidence.note: Airliners designed for rapid conversion could supply much of a bomber's capability while remaining outside a simple ban, making enforceable limits on air power difficult to define.
Restricting bombers raised similar definitional problems for fighters and ground-attack aircraft, illustrating the category disputes and loopholes that also complicated naval treaties.

segments.summary: The difficulty of defining and banning bombers shows why interwar arms-control agreements became blunt instruments, a problem that helps explain the compromises and loopholes surrounding naval treaties.

segments.title: Small battleship studies as a political exercise
segments.body: The United States favored retaining the Washington limits of 35,000 tons and sixteen-inch guns, while Japan wanted the same tonnage and was unwilling to go below fourteen-inch weapons. British naval intelligence and Admiralty debates followed those positions in detail. Against that knowledge, extensive work on lightly protected ten-, eleven-, and twelve-inch battleships is difficult to read as the fleet's preferred operational program. One possible explanation is that complete tables and drawings for the smaller schemes let the naval staff show ministers that it had prepared for their desired treaty outcome. If negotiations failed, the staff could acknowledge the political effort and move to a more credible design that was ready but less visible in the surviving record. This interpretation explains why the best-documented studies may be the least representative of what professional officers actually wanted to fight.

evidence.note: Because British officials knew the United States wanted to retain 35,000-ton ships with 16-inch guns and Japan would not accept less than 14-inch weapons, the smallest British studies may have demonstrated political compliance rather than the fleet's preferred design.
The transcript interprets the surviving tables and drawings as a political exercise alongside an undocumented practical design.

segments.summary: British intelligence knew the United States and Japan would resist the smallest treaty limits, supporting the interpretation that many surviving studies demonstrated political compliance rather than the fleet's preferred warship.

segments.title: Design 12L hints at a fast battleship fallback
segments.body: Design 12L carried nine twelve-inch guns in three triple turrets and a very large battery of high-angle 4.7-inch weapons. Its roughly 27,700-ton hull and 80,000-shaft-horsepower machinery were credited with twenty-seven knots, much faster than the slow sixteen-inch and fourteen-inch studies. A somewhat longer and heavier development could probably approach twenty-eight knots without an extreme increase in power. The design therefore demonstrates that British constructors were already exploring the machinery and hull proportions needed for a fast capital ship even inside a reduced treaty proposal. Design 12L is a clue rather than proof of the missing preferred design: a more credible fallback could borrow its speed while restoring heavier guns and protection. Opening the video here shows how performance data from an apparently political study can reveal the technical options available behind it.

evidence.note: Design 12L combined nine 12-inch guns, roughly 27,700 tons, 80,000 shaft horsepower, and 27-knot speed; a modestly longer and heavier development might have approached 28 knots.
The transcript suggests that the fast practical option may have drawn on the 80,000-shaft-horsepower design work visible in the surviving studies.

segments.summary: The 1928 Design 12L paired nine twelve-inch guns with 80,000 shaft horsepower and twenty-seven-knot speed, showing that the reduced treaty studies could still supply the hull and machinery basis for a faster fallback.

segments.title: Renewed escalation dooms the small treaty battleships
segments.body: The comparison uses later escalation as a stress test without claiming that the designers already knew which ships would appear. A fleet centered on lightly protected ten-, eleven-, or twelve-inch battleships could not answer Bismarck or Tirpitz, and Yamato would make the mismatch still more extreme. Britain would then face a panic program to restore heavy capital-ship capability after having spent years and money on ships unable to meet the threat. The example reinforces the central condition behind the small designs: they work only if existing heavy ships disappear and every major power continues to accept comparable limits. It turns abstract treaty tonnage into a concrete procurement-risk scenario.

evidence.note: The transcript uses Bismarck, Tirpitz, and Yamato as later counterfactual tests of the small treaty battleships and predicts emergency replacement construction.

segments.summary: Later ships such as Bismarck, Tirpitz, and Yamato provide a counterfactual stress test showing how rapidly Britain's small treaty battleships would become untenable if other powers resumed heavy construction.

segments.title: Design studies build institutional memory before the King George V class
segments.body: The later King George V class did not emerge from a standing start: its protection, speed, armament arrangement, and turret-layout decisions had a long design ancestry. Interwar studies let British constructors test whether a third turret belonged amidships, farther forward in a Nelson-like arrangement, or aft in a more conventional layout. Britain, the United States, Japan, and Italy maintained active design work even when construction slowed. France suffered from political interruptions, while the Treaty of Versailles prevented Germany from continuing battleship studies and systematically broke up the teams that had done them. That loss was human as well as industrial because experienced people retired without training successors or preserving organizational memory. Paper designs could strengthen a navy even when none of the particular ships was built.

evidence.note: Interwar design experiments and changing turret layouts fed into the later King George V class.
Continuous British naval design work preserved teams and institutional memory that French interruptions and German losses eroded.

segments.summary: Repeated interwar studies trained British design teams and tested layouts that fed into later capital ships, while countries with interrupted design institutions paid a human as well as industrial cost.

segments.title: Infrastructure limits the Royal Navy's unconstrained battleship
segments.body: A global fleet had to fit existing docks and draw on bases, repair facilities, fuel, and other support around the world. Those physical limits make an unrestricted British design very different from an impractical eighty- or hundred-thousand-ton giant. The estimate offered here is a ship of roughly 45,000 to 50,000 tons, designed for twenty-eight to thirty knots and probably mounting nine sixteen-inch guns. Belt protection might rise to about fifteen inches, somewhat heavier than the later King George V class. In broad terms, the result resembles an enlarged and better-protected Lion-class concept. Removing a treaty ceiling would still leave the infrastructure ceiling governing where a capital ship could operate.

evidence.note: Dock, base, repair, and supply limits point toward an unrestricted British battleship of roughly 45,000 to 50,000 tons, 28 to 30 knots, and probably nine 16-inch guns rather than an impractically large design.
The transcript estimates the displacement, speed, armament, and protection of a preferred unrestricted Royal Navy design.

segments.summary: Even without treaty limits, dockyards and global basing would constrain a Royal Navy battleship to a practical fast design of roughly 45,000 to 50,000 tons with sixteen-inch guns.

segments.title: Cruisers and overseas bases make global battle-fleet deployment possible
segments.body: A fleet's peacetime location did not define where it could operate in war. Cruisers maintained routine British presence because they were cheaper to deploy, while battleships could be concentrated for major operations and still be supported abroad. The First World War examples of Coronel, the Falkland Islands, the Channel, and the Mediterranean show that the Grand Fleet's concentration in home waters did not exhaust Britain's global naval reach. Singapore's interwar facilities likewise mattered because they were intended to support a fleet sent east, and their capture gave Japan the infrastructure Britain had built for that purpose.

evidence.note: Cruisers maintained presence while the battle fleet concentrated for war, as First World War deployments around Coronel and the Falkland Islands illustrate.
Singapore's docks and support facilities were built to sustain a British fleet sent east, so their capture transferred to Japan infrastructure intended for that deployment.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy maintained everyday global presence with cruisers while relying on overseas bases and support infrastructure to concentrate its battle fleet wherever a major war required it.

segments.title: Chatfield's fourteen-inch gamble points toward a nine-gun alternative
segments.body: Chatfield's King George V concept depended on three quadruple fourteen-inch turrets delivering a weight of fire comparable to nine sixteen-inch guns. The gamble failed because quadruple mountings proved heavier and more complicated than expected, preventing the intended twelve-gun battery from working as planned. Chatfield was among the few officers willing to accept the smaller calibre. An unconstrained Royal Navy would therefore have been unlikely to accept anything below sixteen-inch weapons. A likely battery was nine guns, combining heavy hitting power with less dependence on the quadruple-turret gamble.

evidence.note: Chatfield tried to match nine sixteen-inch guns with twelve fourteen-inch weapons, but quadruple turrets imposed weight and complexity problems.
The Royal Navy's preferred unrestricted design likely carried nine sixteen-inch guns.

segments.summary: Admiral Chatfield hoped twelve fourteen-inch guns would match the weight of fire of nine sixteen-inch weapons, but the difficulty of quadruple turrets strengthens the case for a preferred British design with nine sixteen-inch guns.

segments.title: Treaty collapse may still produce one restrained generation
segments.body: This is an explicit counterfactual about what follows if the Washington treaty system ends without a successful London agreement. The Royal Navy probably had plans for heavier sixteen-inch-gun ships ready, but the government might initially insist on nominally treaty-sized construction. A first generation near 35,000 tons would signal continued British restraint and express the hope that other powers kept the old limits voluntarily. That policy would become difficult to sustain as soon as foreign navies visibly ignored the ceiling. Political caution could therefore delay the operational response to an arms-control collapse even when the design organization had prepared alternatives.

evidence.note: The transcript considers the British building response if the treaty system broke down after 1930.

segments.summary: If no London settlement extended the treaty system, British politicians might still hold the first new battleships near the old 35,000-ton limit in hope that other navies reciprocated, before foreign escalation forced larger construction.

segments.title: Diving-shell research creates a gunnery safe-zone dilemma
segments.body: Royal Navy researchers studied shells that fell short, entered the water, and continued toward a battleship below the normal armor belt. They compared impact angle, remaining velocity, and underwater travel at different ranges to understand where a diving shell could still cause serious damage. The results informed the placement of additional armor and watertight compartments in both modernizations and new construction. At a steep angle from long range, a shell could retain damaging velocity farther below the surface than a shallower shot. The data also suggested an intermediate range band in which this particular underwater threat might be reduced. A gunnery officer could seek that safer band, but the opponent received the same protection, turning the research into a tactical dilemma rather than a simple ideal range.

evidence.note: Diving-shell research influenced armor placement, watertight subdivision, refits, and new construction.
Underwater shell velocity varied by angle and range, producing an apparent safe zone that benefited both opponents.

segments.summary: Royal Navy experiments tracked shells after water entry to guide underwater armor, subdivision, and gunnery range choices, but any apparent safe zone also benefited the opponent.
